analysis.one_liner: Requires businesses, employers, and governments to make their websites and apps accessible to people with disabilities, under uniform federal standards.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in either House committee it was referred to, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have spelled out that the Americans with Disabilities Act covers websites and apps: any employer, public agency, store, or testing company offering goods, services, or jobs online would have to make those sites and apps usable by people who are blind, deaf, or have other disabilities — including services offered only online. The Justice Department and the EEOC would write one set of national accessibility standards instead of the current patchwork of conflicting court rulings, and people with disabilities could sue to enforce the rules. Companies facing an undue burden could get an exemption, and a technical assistance center would help businesses comply.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities — including those who are blind, deaf, hard of hearing, or have mobility or speech disabilities — would gain equal access to the jobs, government services, shopping, banking, education, and testing that now happen mostly online. The bill's own findings describe a situation in which most websites and apps contain significant barriers, leaving disabled people excluded from equal participation in society and treated, in its words, as second-class citizens. Workers with disabilities would also benefit in hiring, since job application systems and training platforms would have to be accessible. Businesses would get one clear national standard to follow instead of conflicting court decisions, plus government-funded technical assistance on how to comply.

how_it_helps.text: It would require employers, governments, public accommodations, and testing entities to make the websites and apps they use to serve the public accessible, with the same ease of use and privacy as everyone else — including services offered only online.

It would direct the Justice Department and the EEOC to write uniform accessibility standards within two years and update them every three, ending the court-by-court confusion that has let many websites stay inaccessible.

It would let people with disabilities sue directly in state or federal court without exhausting administrative remedies, and let the Attorney General seek civil penalties and compensatory and punitive damages on their behalf.

It would fund a technical assistance center ($15 million a year for fiscal 2024–2028) to help entities build accessible websites and apps, and create a standing advisory committee whose majority must be people with disabilities.
It would cover the software vendors themselves: commercial providers that design or build websites and apps for covered entities could not deliver inaccessible products.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that operate online would pay the most: redesigning and maintaining accessible websites, apps, kiosks, and hiring systems, and potential damages and legal fees if sued. The cost would fall hardest on small businesses, and the bill also authorized up to $20 million a year in federal spending for enforcement and a technical assistance center. Employers and testing companies would face the same obligations for online hiring and examinations.

drawbacks.text: Nearly every business that operates online — retailers, banks, restaurants, streaming services — would have had to redesign or remediate websites and apps to meet DOJ standards, a cost that falls hardest on smaller firms with thin margins, though the bill does allow an 'undue burden' defense.

The bill lets individuals sue in court without first notifying or giving the business a chance to fix the problem, and awards attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs, which critics of ADA website litigation warn invites demand-letter and lawsuit abuse against small businesses.

It authorized $5 million a year for rulemaking and enforcement plus $15 million a year for a technical assistance center, spending that opponents of new mandates would flag as an added federal expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and the bill was carefully built: it set concrete standards after decades of legal uncertainty, gave small and struggling entities an undue-burden defense, funded technical assistance so businesses could comply, and let individuals sue without jumping through notification hoops. The main costs are compliance spending across a huge swath of the economy and the risk of litigation by serial plaintiffs, since the bill bars any rule requiring people to complain to a business before suing — an honest supporter would acknowledge that exposure and that small businesses would feel the compliance burden most. On balance, the bill traded real, recurring exclusion of disabled people from jobs, government services, and commerce for costs that appear manageable, especially with the built-in defenses and assistance program.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2022, sent to two House committees, referred to a Judiciary subcommittee six weeks later, and neither committee ever scheduled it for consideration before the Congress ended in early January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on September 28, 2022 and referred to the Education and Labor Committee and the Judiciary Committee.
On November 1, 2022 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties — the last action recorded before the Congress ended.
No markup, hearing, or floor vote is recorded for the bill at any point in the 117th Congress.
It attracted 9 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no version was introduced in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses with digital-only or largely digital services are better off: they face no binding federal accessibility standard and no new litigation exposure, and people with disabilities remain without a uniform, enforceable right of access.

for.name: 9 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on November 1, 2022 and never scheduled it for markup or a vote; the referral was the committee's last action on the bill.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration after the September 2022 referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Business groups opposing ADA website litigation
against.what_they_did: Have long pressed Congress and the Justice Department against new binding website accessibility rules and expanded private lawsuits, arguing existing law is vague and fuels drive-by suits.

sides.party_line_note: All ten supporters in the House were Democrats (the sponsor plus 9 cosponsors) and no Republican backed it, but the bill never reached a vote, so partisan positioning on it was never actually tested.

industries.industry: E-commerce, banking, streaming, and other online businesses
industries.note: These firms would have to redesign and remediate websites and apps to meet new federal accessibility standards, with lawsuits available without prior notice. For ordinary people this is the flip side of the benefit: the cost of equal access to online goods and services falls on the companies selling them.

industries.industry: Web design, software development, and accessibility remediation vendors
industries.note: Commercial providers that build websites and apps for covered entities would be directly liable for delivering inaccessible products, but the mandate and the funded technical assistance program would also create steady demand for accessibility expertise. Compliance work would become a growth business.

industries.industry: Employers with online hiring and HR systems
industries.note: Job applications, training portals, and internal tools would have to be usable by disabled applicants and employees, enforceable by the EEOC and private lawsuits. Disabled job seekers would gain; companies would bear the cost of retrofitting their hiring software.

Providers of exams and professional certification courses offered online would have to make them accessible. That removes a barrier to employment credentials for disabled people, at the testing companies' expense.

Public entities would have to make all online services, programs, and information accessible, with federal funding limited to a technical assistance center. The burden of compliance lands on government budgets and, indirectly, taxpayers.
